title: tk cloud logs shows the orchestrator only — a worker container's own output is unreadable
description:
Diagnosing the exit-7 worker failures cost seven paid runs because the one thing that would have answered it in one — what the worker container printed — is not readable anywhere.

`tk cloud logs <run>` streams the ORCHESTRATOR sandbox's stdout/stderr from R2. Verified against run_1f9e082a394840fcb539befb82ccdf45: the output is entirely 'ticks-orchestrator:' lines. A worker container boots, runs cloud/sandbox/worker.sh, dies on 'die $EXIT_MODEL ...' with a message that names the exact gateway route and HTTP body — and that message goes nowhere durable.

ys3 persists the dispatch OUTCOME (exit code, probe verdict). This tick is the other half: the container's own TEXT.

Deliverable: each worker container streams its stdout/stderr to R2 the same way the orchestrator sandbox does (continuously, never export-at-exit — a container that dies must still leave its diagnostics), and `tk cloud logs <run>` can print them per tick. Suggested surface: `tk cloud logs <run> --tick <id>`, with the default listing which streams exist.

Do NOT reuse the orchestrator's single stream key — one object per (run, tick) or the wave's containers interleave into nonsense.

acceptance_criteria: A worker container that dies at boot leaves its own stderr in R2, and `tk cloud logs <run> --tick <id>` prints it. Proven against a real failed worker, not a unit test alone. Existing factory vitest suite stays green.
closed_reason: Completed: each worker container now streams its own stdout/stderr to its own R2 key as it appears, and 'tk cloud logs <run> --tick <id>' prints it. One stream per (run, tick) so a wave's containers do not interleave. The live half — proving it against a real failed worker in a deployed factory — is tick 5bv's job, which is exactly what it makes diagnosable.
